prompt: Why does `writeJSON` call `json.Marshal` before writing anything to `w`?
hint: What has already left once the first byte of the body is sent?

choices.text: Because `json.Marshal` is faster than writing to the connection byte by byte through an encoder
choices.why: Speed is not the reason the section gives; the order of status and body is.

choices.text: Because a `ResponseWriter` refuses a write of more than one line
choices.why: It accepts any bytes, in as many writes as you like.

choices.text: So that a value that cannot be encoded still becomes an honest 500 with nothing sent
choices.why: Right. Encoding into memory first means nothing was sent yet when it fails.

choices.text: So that the `Content-Length` header comes out right
choices.why: `net/http` works out the length either way for a small body; the reason is the status.

prompt: `Event` has the tag `json:"id"` on its `ID` field. What does a client see without that tag?
hint: Where does the default key name come from?

choices.text: The key `ID`, spelled the way the Go field is spelled
choices.why: Right. Legal, and unusual enough that clients in other languages trip over it.

choices.text: The key `id`, because `encoding/json` lowercases names by itself
choices.why: It does not change the case; the tag is what makes it `id`.

choices.text: No `ID` at all, because untagged fields are skipped
choices.why: Exported fields are encoded with or without a tag.

choices.text: A compile error in `writeJSON`
choices.why: Tags are read at run time; nothing about them is checked by the compiler.

prompt: The answer for event 1 is one flat object with `available` beside `id` and `sold`. How did `available` get there?
hint: Look at `eventView`.

choices.text: The store saves it with every sale
choices.why: The store keeps `Seats` and `Sold`; nothing stores what is left.

choices.text: `json.Marshal` computes it from the tags
choices.why: Tags rename fields; they compute nothing.

choices.text: The client adds it after reading `seats` and `sold`
choices.why: It is in the bytes the server sent.

choices.text: `eventView` embeds `Event` and adds it, and embedded fields appear as the outer struct's own
choices.why: Right. Worked out as `Seats - Sold` when the answer is built.

prompt: An export endpoint returns four hundred megabytes of rows. Which way of writing JSON does the lesson point it to, and at what price?
hint: Holding everything in memory first is what `writeJSON` does.

choices.text: `writeJSON`, because an honest 500 matters more than memory
choices.why: For megabytes of rows the lesson prefers streaming.

choices.text: Streaming with `json.NewEncoder(w)`, accepting that a failure shows up as a truncated body
choices.why: Right. The error arrives after the 200, and the client has to notice the cut.

choices.text: Streaming, which also lets the server change the status if it fails
choices.why: The status left with the first bytes; nothing changes it after that.

choices.text: Neither: JSON is refused above one mebibyte
choices.why: The 1 MiB limit is on request bodies read by `decodeJSON`, not on responses.

prompt: A client misspells `quantity` as `quantiy`. What does the one-liner `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&p)` do with it?
hint: What does a plain decoder do with a field the struct lacks?

choices.text: Drops it silently
choices.why: Right. The purchase becomes zero tickets with no complaint; `DisallowUnknownFields` turns it into an error.

choices.text: Returns a syntax error with the byte offset of the misspelled key
choices.why: The JSON is valid; only the name is unknown.

choices.text: Guesses the closest field and fills `Quantity`
choices.why: `encoding/json` matches names, case-insensitively, and never by similarity.

choices.text: Panics inside the handler
choices.why: Decoding returns errors; it does not panic.

prompt: Why does `decodeJSON` call `dec.Decode(&struct{}{})` a second time after the first `Decode` succeeded?
hint: `{"quantity": 2}{"quantity": 9}`.

choices.text: To check the first object again with stricter rules
choices.why: The first object is done; the second call looks past it.

choices.text: To read the rest of the body so the connection can be reused by the next request
choices.why: Its purpose is the check: anything other than the end is refused.

choices.text: It has to find the end of the input, and anything else after the object is refused
choices.why: Right. Anything after the object, even another valid object, is refused.

choices.text: To decode the `email` field, which the first call skips
choices.why: One `Decode` fills every field of the struct.

prompt: How many bytes long was the limit in the refusal of the two-million-character body?
`{"quantity": 2,}` was refused as not valid JSON at which byte?
hint: The offset points at the `}` after the comma.

prompt: Match each body sent to `POST /events/1/tickets` with the `detail` it got.
hint: Which case of the `switch` caught each?

pairs.right: the body ends in the middle of a JSON value
the field "quantity" has the wrong type: want int
the body has an unknown field "seat"

prompt: Why does the unknown-field case of `decodeJSON` test the error's text with `strings.HasPrefix` instead of `errors.As`?
hint: What type does `encoding/json` give that error?

choices.text: `errors.As` is slower and the decoder runs on every request
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Because the message has to be translated before it reaches the client
choices.why: The text is reworded, but that is not why it is matched by prefix.

choices.text: `DisallowUnknownFields` returns a `*json.SyntaxError`, which the case above already caught
choices.why: If it did, the syntax case would have answered; it did not.

choices.text: It has no type of its own to match
choices.why: Right. `encoding/json` reports an unknown field only as a plain message.

prompt: `{}` is sent to buy tickets. Why is the answer 422 and not 400?
hint: Did the body decode?

choices.text: An empty object is not valid JSON, and 422 is the status for broken JSON
choices.why: `{}` is valid JSON, and broken JSON gets 400 in boxoffice.

choices.text: The store refused it because event 1 has no seats
choices.why: The store was never reached; and event 1 had 120 seats.

choices.text: It decoded; the zero values failed the checks
choices.why: Right. `0` and `""` are read fine and then refused by `validate`.

choices.text: The mux turned a 400 into a 422
choices.why: The mux writes only its own 404 and 405.

prompt: Why does `validate` collect every problem into a map instead of returning at the first one?
hint: Think of the client fixing its request.

choices.text: A map is the only type `writeProblem` accepts
choices.why: It accepts nil too; the map is a choice about the client.

choices.text: Go maps keep their keys in insertion order
choices.why: They have no order; `encoding/json` sorts the keys when it writes them.

choices.text: So that one answer names every mistake, instead of making the client send one request per mistake
choices.why: Right. `{"quantity": 40, "email": "ana"}` got both fields named at once.

choices.text: Returning early would skip the store
choices.why: A failed validation skips the store anyway, on purpose.

prompt: A new field `discount` may legitimately be `0`, and leaving it out must mean "use the default". How does the lesson say to declare it?
hint: `encoding/json` cannot tell a missing field from one sent as zero.

choices.text: As `int` with `omitempty`
choices.why: `omitempty` affects writing, not reading; a missing field still reads as 0.

choices.text: As a string, parsed by hand in `validate`
choices.why: That changes the JSON type the client has to send; a pointer keeps it a number.

choices.text: As `int`, and treat 0 as missing
choices.why: Then a real discount of 0 is indistinguishable from none.

choices.text: As `*int`
choices.why: Right. It stays `nil` when the key is missing and points at 0 when 0 was sent.

prompt: What does `strings.Contains(p.Email, "@")` check, according to the lesson?
hint: What is the only real test of an address?

choices.text: That a name was not typed into the wrong box, and nothing more
choices.why: Right. Weak on purpose: stricter patterns reject real addresses and still let typos through.

choices.text: That the address exists
choices.why: Only sending a message tests that.

choices.text: That the address follows RFC 5322
choices.why: One `@` says nothing about the full grammar.

choices.text: That the domain accepts mail
choices.why: No network is consulted.

prompt: Put the checks of `buyTickets` in the order it runs them.
hint: Cheapest first.
items: `pathID` reads the id in the path
trap: `/events/nine/tickets` got a 400 before the body was looked at.

prompt: What media type does `writeProblem` send?
hint: RFC 9457 has one of its own.

choices.text: `application/json`
choices.why: That is `writeJSON`'s default, which `writeProblem` sets before calling it.

choices.text: `text/plain; charset=utf-8`
choices.why: That is what `http.Error` and the mux's own 404 and 405 send.

choices.text: `application/problem+json`
choices.why: Right. `writeJSON` keeps a `Content-Type` that is already set.

choices.text: `application/error+json`
choices.why: No such type is in the RFC.

prompt: An unexpected database error reaches `fail`. What `detail` does the client receive?
hint: The `default` case.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Right. The `detail` is empty and left out; the status 500 is all the client gets.

choices.text: The error's message, so the client can report it
choices.why: The message can name a file, a query or a host; it goes to the log.

choices.text: A stack trace, as `recoverPanics` logs
choices.why: The stack goes to the log, never into a response.

choices.text: `about:blank`
choices.why: That is the `type`, not the `detail`.

prompt: In `catchall`, `DELETE /events` answered 404 with a JSON body. What did the catch-all pattern `/` cost?
hint: Before it was registered, what did the mux answer for that request?

choices.text: Nothing: the mux writes a JSON 404 by itself for wrong methods
choices.why: The mux writes a text 405 for a wrong method, as boxoffice still shows.

choices.text: The `GET /events` route, which `/` replaced
choices.why: `GET /events` still answered `every event`; it is more specific.

choices.text: The honest 405 and its `Allow` header, because `/` now matches every path and method
choices.why: Right. The mux always finds a pattern, so it never says the method is wrong.

choices.text: A panic at start, because `/` conflicts with `GET /events`
choices.why: One is more specific, so there is no conflict; the server ran.

prompt: Match each member of a problem details object to what it holds.
hint: The table of section 05.

pairs.right: a URI naming the kind of problem
the same short summary for every occurrence
this occurrence, in words a developer can act on
boxoffice's extension: problems field by field

right_distractors: the stack trace of the failure

prompt: When the status says it all, the `type` of a problem is ___.
hint: A URI that points nowhere.

prompt: Why does the store return `ErrSoldOut` instead of an HTTP 409?
hint: Who else will call the store?

choices.text: Callers without HTTP will use it
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL in lesson 6 and gRPC in lesson 10 have no 404 or 409.

choices.text: Because a Go function is not allowed to import `net/http` outside `main`
choices.why: Any package may import it; the store chooses not to speak HTTP.

choices.text: 409 does not exist in `net/http`
choices.why: `http.StatusConflict` is 409, and `fail` uses it.

choices.text: Errors are faster to compare than status codes
choices.why: The reason is who speaks which vocabulary.

prompt: Why does `fail` use `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` rather than `err == ErrNotFound`?
hint: What will the store do to its errors from lesson 6 on?

choices.text: It also matches a wrapped error
choices.why: Right. `==` would miss the wrapped error and answer 500.

choices.text: `==` does not compile on two errors
choices.why: It compiles; errors are interfaces and comparable.

choices.text: `errors.Is` ignores the case of the message
choices.why: It compares error values, never messages.

choices.text: `==` compares the messages, which change between versions
choices.why: `==` compares the values themselves.

prompt: Why is a purchase that does not fit a 409 Conflict rather than a 422?
hint: Would the same request ever succeed?

choices.text: The values are invalid, and 409 is the newer name for 422
choices.why: They are distinct statuses; the values here are valid.

choices.text: Valid request, conflicting with the event's current state
choices.why: Right. A refund that frees seats could make the same request succeed tomorrow.

choices.text: Because the store returned it before `validate` ran
choices.why: `validate` runs first; the store is last.

choices.text: Because 409 tells the client to retry immediately in a loop
choices.why: Nothing in 409 says that.

prompt: `Sell` reads the event, checks the seats and writes, all under the write lock. What goes wrong if it released the lock between the check and the write?
hint: Two buyers, one seat.

choices.text: Both read one seat left, both pass, both are sold it
choices.why: Right. Holding the lock from read to write makes the sale all or nothing.

choices.text: The second buyer waits forever for the lock that was released
choices.why: A released lock is free to take; nobody waits forever.

choices.text: The map panics because it is read and written by the same goroutine twice in a row
choices.why: One goroutine reading and writing a map is fine.

choices.text: Nothing, because `ErrSoldOut` is a sentinel
choices.why: A sentinel names the refusal; it does not prevent the race.

prompt: After the first purchase of 2 tickets for event 1, how many seats did `remaining` report?
hint: Event 1 has 120 seats.

prompt: The manager creates the Organ Recital. Besides 201, what tells the client where to read the new event?
hint: A header.

choices.text: `Content-Location: /admin/events/3`, the address of the staff copy
choices.why: boxoffice sends `Location`, pointing at the public route.

choices.text: `Location: /events/3`
choices.why: Right. That is what 201 promises a client.

choices.text: A `link` field inside the JSON body of the answer
choices.why: The body is the event's view; it carries no link.

choices.text: Nothing; the client has to list every event and look for it
choices.why: The `Location` header was there in the capture.

prompt: The door token posts a new event. Who refuses it, and with what?
hint: The token is real.

choices.text: `requireManager`, with a 403 problem
choices.why: Right. `only a manager may do this`, as `application/problem+json`.

choices.text: `requireStaff`, with a 401 problem
choices.why: The token is known, so `requireStaff` lets it through.

choices.text: `validate`, with a 422 listing the role as an invalid field
choices.why: The role check runs before the body is read.

choices.text: The mux, with a text 405
choices.why: `POST /admin/events` is registered.

prompt: After lesson 3, which of these answers does boxoffice send as `application/problem+json`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two middlewares were changed; the mux was not.

choices.text: the 401 from `requireStaff`
choices.why: Right. It now calls `writeProblem`.

choices.text: the 500 from `recoverPanics`
choices.why: Right, with no `detail`.

choices.text: the 405 for `DELETE /events`
choices.why: The mux writes that one, in plain text.

choices.text: the 409 for the sold-out Chamber Choir
choices.why: Right. `fail` maps `ErrSoldOut` to it.

choices.text: the 201 receipt of a purchase
choices.why: A success is plain `application/json`.

prompt: The server is stopped and started again. What is left of the Organ Recital and the two tickets sold?
hint: Where does the store keep them?

choices.text: Both survive, because `writeJSON` wrote them to disk
choices.why: `writeJSON` writes to the response, nowhere else.

choices.text: Nothing of either: both lived in a map in memory
choices.why: Right. The store is a map in memory; lesson 6 puts it in PostgreSQL.

choices.text: The event survives but the sale does not
choices.why: Both live in the same map.

choices.text: Whatever the server's log recorded is replayed at start
choices.why: The log is read by people, not by boxoffice.

hint: The path, the body, the values, the seats.

prompt: A client sends `{"quantity": 2, "email": "ana@example.com"}` to `/events/2/tickets` and then `{"Quantity": 2}` to `/events/1/tickets`. What does it get?
hint: Event 2 is the Chamber Choir. `encoding/json` matches names case-insensitively.

choices.text: 409, then 422 for the missing e-mail
choices.why: Right. Sold out first; then `Quantity` fills `quantity` and only `email` is missing.

choices.text: 409, then 400 for an unknown field `Quantity`
choices.why: The decoder matches `Quantity` to the `quantity` tag, so it is not unknown.
Event 2 exists; it is sold out.

choices.text: 201 twice, since both bodies are valid JSON objects with a quantity of two
choices.why: Valid JSON is the first step of four.
